_what: THE ONE LIST of everything a client can do with Wingguy. Two things are generated from it by utils/wingguyCapabilities.js and there is no second copy of the words: the SHORT answer to "what can I do with Wingguy?" (wingguy_vision in services/wingguyGetStartedMcp.js) and the FULL page at knowaguy.com.au/what-wingguy-can-do (routes/marketingRoutes.js). Checked by tests/wingguy-capabilities.test.js.
_why: 9 Nov 2026: the answer a brand-new client got on onboarding day never mentioned their Linked Helper machine, still said leads arrive by copy and paste, and was missing half of what had been built since July. It was hand-written prose, so nothing made it keep up. Now a new tool cannot ship without a line here - the test fails until it has one.
_rules: Built a new tool? Add it to an item's tools here (or a new item), or to not_shown with the reason. Then run: node tests/wingguy-capabilities.test.js

say: the sentence the client types. It must already be in content/client-phrases.json when the item has tools - that is the house rule for any sentence a client is told to type, and the test enforces it.
does: what it DOES, in Guy's plain English, before what it is called. Short dash ' - ', never an em dash. Say 'instructions', never 'rules'. No praise of Wingguy's own drafting.
tools: every MCP tool that sits behind this line. The first one is the tool the say-sentence must be registered against.
needs: machine | mailbox | calendar | notes - when the client has not connected that yet, the line is still shown, marked as opening up once they do.
added: YYYY-MM-DD for a new feature. The line carries a 'New' flag for 30 days from that date, then drops it by itself.
not_shown: tools deliberately left out of the client answer (Guy-only, or the answer itself), each with the reason.

The sections ARE THE STORY (Guy, 10 Nov 2026): ten steps in the order a stranger becomes someone you know. The page shows every step's lead in full and folds the sentences under it. A new section is a new step in that story - put it where it happens, not at the end.

lead: the step told in Guy's voice, explaining its own terms the moment they appear (Linked Helper, campaign, scored) - a reader who has never heard of any of it must be able to follow. Claims about how good Wingguy is stay third person ('Guy reckons').
short (per section): one plain line - the step's summary in the chat answer and on the page's map.
start: true on the handful of lines a brand-new client should try first - they make the 'first day' strip near the foot of the page.

sections.title: You choose who you want to know
sections.short: A LinkedIn search: the kind of people, the kind of job, the place.
sections.lead: It starts with a search on LinkedIn - the kind of people you want in your network, the kind of job they do, where they are. That search is the only thing in this whole system that only you can do, because only you know who belongs. I help you build it.

items.say: help me work out who to search for
items.does: we work out the search together - who, what title, where - and I show you how to set it up on LinkedIn.

items.say: Who should I be connecting with?
items.does: Guy's answer, in his words - who is worth your network and who isn't.

sections.title: A machine invites them for you
sections.short: A computer in the cloud that Guy looks after sends your connection requests, every day, by itself.
sections.lead: It's a computer in the cloud that Guy sets up and looks after, running software called **Linked Helper**. Every day it sends your connection request, with your note, to a few of the people from your search - up to 100 a week, spread over working hours so it looks like a real person at work. That list of people and the note it sends is your **campaign**. You never log in to it. It's checked every day and backed up every night, and if LinkedIn ever signs you out you get an email. When it runs low on people, you give it a new search.

items.does: invitations sent, how many said yes, and how many people are still waiting. The same numbers land in your inbox every Monday.
see the message it sends, the days and times it runs and how many go out a week - then change any of it in plain English. I show you the change before I make it.

items.say: top up my campaign with this search
items.does: paste a LinkedIn search link and I add those people, so it never runs dry.
every campaign your leads are coming from, and how many each has brought in.
your own link, straight in from any browser.

items.say: put this file on my machine
items.does: get a file or a line of text from your computer onto the machine without any fiddling.

sections.title: Everyone who says yes lands in Wingguy
sections.short: Read, scored against who you are after, best first.
sections.lead: When someone accepts, they show up in your leads by themselves - nothing to copy or type. Their profile is read and they're **scored** against who you're really after, so the best people come first and you never work through a list in the order it arrived.

items.does: change what a good lead looks like for you, test it on real people before anything is saved, and undo it if you don't like it.

items.say: who is Sarah and what's her email?
items.does: one lookup across your leads and everyone you've written to.
someone you met another way, or a person you've just been introduced to, goes in properly. Fix a city, email or phone the same way, or tag people into a list.
the website where you work your leads.

sections.title: You thank them, and the conversation starts
sections.short: A note from their real profile in about thirty seconds, sounding like you.
sections.lead: This is the moment it clicks. I write the thanks-for-connecting note from their real profile and what they post - not a template. What would have taken you ten minutes takes about thirty seconds, and Guy reckons it sounds like you, not like AI. You read it and send it. And if a line isn't quite you, say so on the spot and it's fixed for every note after.

items.does: off their real profile and what they post, on your instructions, never a template.

items.say: What do I say to thank someone for connecting?
items.does: Guy's method for the first message - why it isn't a pitch, and what it is instead.

sections.title: Wingguy keeps every conversation moving
sections.short: Who you owe a reply, worked out overnight, drafts ready.
sections.lead: Nobody falls through the cracks. Every night I work out who you owe something - a reply, a nudge, a promised note - and write the drafts, so when you sit down the list is ready. The people you already know are on it too: old conversations worth picking up again are worth more than any new name.

items.does: everyone you owe something, best first, with the drafts already written. Park someone until a date, or drop them for good.
your whole history with anyone in one go - calls, emails, LinkedIn, what you agreed last time.
rebuild the list right now if a lot has changed.
the people who went quiet months ago, sorted into worth reopening and let go, with the reopening notes written.
the people you already know on LinkedIn are worth the most. I find the old conversations worth picking up and bring you a few each day.

sections.title: When it moves to email, I write the email
sections.short: Drafts in your own mailbox. You press send.
sections.lead: Every email goes into your own mailbox as a draft, on the right thread, links intact. I never send - that is always you. I can read what they wrote back, show you the whole back-and-forth with one person, and go through your inbox with you.

items.does: a real draft in your Drafts folder, links intact, on the right thread.

items.say: what did she say in her last email?
items.does: I read it to you, or show the whole back-and-forth with one person and what you've already sent them.
sorted into what needs you, what's just for your info and what can go. Clearing them out works on Gmail today, and nothing goes without your yes.

sections.title: When they want to meet, I book it
sections.short: Real free times from your diary, offered and booked.
sections.lead: I read your real calendar, apply your hours, your buffers and both time zones, and offer times that actually work. When they pick one, the invite, your meeting link and the reminders all go out. Before the call, I brief you on who you're meeting.

items.does: today's diary plus everything I know about who you're meeting. Guy starts every morning this way.
three real slots that suit you both - and if they sent a booking link, I read it and find where you overlap.
which days, what times, how much gap between meetings and how many a day - it is your diary, so you decide.
the invite, your meeting link and the reminders, all sent. Move or cancel it later just by saying so.

sections.title: After the call, the follow-up writes itself
sections.short: Every recorded call kept against the right person.
sections.lead: If a note-taker is on the call, the transcript is filed against the right person and I write the follow-up from what was actually said - the thing you promised, the name they mentioned, the next step you agreed. You never open a transcript. It's your data: you can see every call I hold and delete any of it.

items.say: draft the follow-up from my last call
items.does: I read the transcript and write the email from what was actually said.

items.say: here's the transcript from a call you missed
items.does: paste it in and I file it against the right person.
see every call I keep, stop one before it's stored, or delete any of it for good. It's your data.

sections.title: It all runs on your instructions, in your words
sections.short: You say how you like things written. It learns from what you change.
sections.lead: Everything above is written on your own instructions - how you open, what you never say, the links you like to share. You change them in plain English, I show you the change before I make it, and it sticks. And whenever you edit one of my drafts before sending, I learn from what you changed.

items.does: a guided chat that turns the starter kit into your voice - your angle, who you're after, how you handle a no.
tell me what to do differently. I show you the change before I make it, it sticks for good, and you can always go back.

items.say: never use the word folks again
items.does: your banned words, gone from every draft.

items.say: add this article to my library
items.does: your own links - articles, videos, your booking page - ready to drop into the right message.
whenever you change one of my drafts before sending, I learn from what you changed and offer to fold it into your instructions.

sections.title: And Guy's whole method is built in
sections.short: Ask how, and you get his answer in his words.
sections.lead: I don't only do the work - I teach you Guy's method as you go: what to say when someone accepts, why the second meeting is the one that matters, how to hold a steady pace. Ask and you get his answer in his words, not generic advice off the internet. What he learns with every client lands in your Wingguy too.

items.does: the guided tour through getting started, picked up wherever you left it.
a quick check of what's connected and what's still to do.
